items.prompt: Read this speech aloud as if you were giving it in assembly. Use pauses and emphasis to persuade your audience.

criteria.label: Reads fluently and accurately
Uses pauses and emphasis to persuade
Changes tone for the question and for the serious points
Sounds confident and sincere

items.readText:
Good morning, everyone. My name is Arya, and I would like to be your next school council representative.
Our school is a wonderful place, but I know we can make it even better. Have you ever waited ten minutes to borrow a football at break? I have. That is why my first promise is simple: a sports box for every class.
My second promise is a suggestion box outside the library, so that every pupil, from Grade 1 to Grade 6, can share ideas.
I will listen carefully, and I will keep the promises I make today. Thank you.
hints: Read the speech silently first and mark the words you want to stress.
Pause after the question so the audience can think.
items.explanation: A persuasive speech is more powerful when the speaker pauses after key points, stresses important words and sounds sincere.

items.prompt: Give a one-minute opening speech for or against this motion: Homework should be optional for primary pupils.

criteria.label: States a clear position on the motion
Gives at least two reasons with examples
Uses persuasive language, including a rhetorical question
Speaks clearly at a good pace
Ends with a strong summary

hints: Begin by saying clearly whether you are for or against the motion.
Signpost your reasons: firstly, secondly, finally.
Finish by repeating your position in one strong sentence.
items.explanation: An opening speech in a debate states a position, supports it with reasons and examples and ends with a clear summary.

items.prompt: Give a short talk explaining why Indonesia has a wet season and a dry season. Your audience is a class of Grade 4 pupils.

criteria.label: Explains the main cause clearly in simple words
Describes the steps in the right order
Uses vocabulary that suits younger listeners
Speaks clearly and keeps the audience interested

hints: Explain one idea at a time: land and sea, then the wind, then the rain.
Replace difficult words with simple ones, or explain them.
items.explanation: A good explanation for younger pupils breaks the process into simple steps and uses words they understand.

items.prompt: Your opponent says: School uniforms stop pupils from expressing themselves. Respond politely, explain why you disagree and give evidence.

criteria.label: Sums up the opponent’s point fairly
Disagrees politely, with phrases such as I understand, however
Gives a clear counter-argument with an example
Stays calm and confident

hints: Start by showing that you have listened: I understand that...
Then give your counter-argument and one example.
items.explanation: A good rebuttal shows respect for the other side, then explains clearly why the point is weak, using evidence.

items.prompt: Tell the same news twice: first to a friend, then to your head teacher. The news is that your class has won a recycling competition.

criteria.label: Uses informal, friendly language with the friend
Uses formal, polite language with the head teacher
Gives the key facts both times
Changes tone of voice to suit each listener

hints: Plan the facts first: what you won, when and how.
Think about greetings: Guess what! for a friend, Good morning for a head teacher.
items.explanation: Speakers change their words and tone for different listeners. The facts stay the same, but the register changes.

items.prompt: Give a short vote of thanks to a visiting author at a school assembly. Mention one thing you learned from the visit.

criteria.label: Uses formal language suitable for an assembly
Thanks the visitor by name and mentions specific details
Is short, clear and well organised
Speaks warmly and confidently

hints: A vote of thanks is short: thank the visitor, mention a highlight and thank them again.
Use the visitor’s name and title.
items.explanation: A vote of thanks is a short, formal speech that thanks a guest and shows that the audience valued the visit.

items.prompt: Argue both sides. Speak for one minute for this motion, then one minute against it: Every school should have a vegetable garden.

criteria.label: Gives strong reasons for the motion
Gives strong reasons against the motion
Uses clear signposts such as firstly and on the other hand
Keeps a fair, confident tone on both sides
Finishes within the time

hints: Plan two reasons for each side before you start.
Use a clear signal when you switch sides, such as On the other hand.
items.explanation: Arguing both sides helps you understand an issue fully and prepares you to answer an opponent in a real debate.

items.prompt: Which phrase is best for politely challenging an opponent in a debate?

options.text: I understand my opponent’s point; however, the evidence shows something different.
That’s rubbish and everyone knows it.
options.why: This is rude and gives no evidence.

options.text: My opponent is wrong because I say so.
options.why: This gives no reason or evidence.

hints: Good debaters are polite even when they disagree.
A strong challenge recognises the other point, then gives evidence.
Find the option that mentions evidence.
items.explanation: The best challenge shows you listened, then uses evidence to disagree. This is more persuasive than rudeness.

items.prompt: Put the stages of a school debate in order.
items: The first speaker for the motion speaks.
The first speaker against the motion speaks.
Each side gives a closing summary.
hints: A debate begins by stating what will be discussed.
Each side speaks in turn before anyone sums up.
Start with the person who runs the debate.
items.explanation: The chair introduces the motion, each side opens, speakers answer each other, each side sums up and finally the audience votes.

items.prompt: You are speaking to parents at a formal school event. Which sentence is most suitable?

options.text: Hey everyone, cool that you turned up!
options.why: This is too casual for a formal event.

options.text: You lot should look at our projects.
options.why: You lot is informal and sounds rude.

options.text: Thank you all for coming this evening to see our science projects.
Um, so, yeah, the projects are over there.

hints: Think about who the audience is and how formal the event is.
Formal speech is polite, clear and complete.
Find the sentence that thanks the audience politely.
items.explanation: At a formal event, a speaker should be polite and clear. Thanking the audience for coming is a good, formal start.
